statement: With homogeneous products and constant marginal cost, price competition between two firms drives the equilibrium price down to marginal cost.
short: A small undercut captures the whole market.
detail: Capacity constraints or product differentiation soften the result.
proof: If both prices exceed cost, either firm gains by slightly undercutting; no price below cost can be optimal.
consequence: It highlights how the strategic variable changes market outcomes.

title: Walrasian Equilibrium and Market Clearing
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: A Walrasian equilibrium consists of prices and allocations such that every agent maximises utility subject to their budget and all markets clear.
short: One price vector makes every plan compatible.
detail: Prices are only defined up to a common positive scalar, reflecting homogeneity.
proof: Given optimising demands and supplies, Walras' law implies that clearing all but one market clearing implies the last clears.
consequence: It is the central solution concept of general equilibrium theory.

title: Arrow–Debreu Existence of General Equilibrium
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: An exchange or production economy with convex preferences, convex production sets, and suitable boundedness has at least one competitive equilibrium.
short: Convexity and continuity guarantee a market-clearing price vector.
detail: The proof relies on fixed-point theorems applied to an excess-demand correspondence.
proof: Normalise prices to the simplex, apply Kakutani's theorem to a truncated excess-demand map, and show the limiting allocation clears markets.
consequence: It provides a rigorous foundation for Adam Smith's invisible hand intuition.

title: First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: Every competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient under local nonsatiation of preferences.
short: Markets leave no mutually beneficial trades unexploited.
detail: It requires complete markets and no externalities or public goods.
proof: If an allocation Pareto dominated it, the budget inequalities and local nonsatiation would imply an impossible inequality after multiplying by equilibrium prices.
consequence: It gives a formal case for market efficiency under ideal conditions.

title: Second Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: Under convexity assumptions, any Pareto efficient allocation can be supported as a competitive equilibrium after a suitable redistribution of initial endowments.
short: Equity and efficiency can be separated in principle.
detail: The required transfers are lump-sum and depend on the desired allocation.
proof: Separate the preferred allocation from the aggregate production set and choose endowments so the resulting budget hyperplane supports it.
consequence: It underpins the theory of redistribution without distorting prices.

title: Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: If a chosen bundle was affordable when another bundle was chosen, the second bundle cannot be affordable when the first is chosen unless choices are identical.
short: Observed choices cannot contradict themselves.
detail: The strong axiom extends the condition to chains of revealed preference.
proof: Assume both bundles were chosen in the two budget situations and derive a contradiction from the maximisation hypothesis.
consequence: It tests whether demand data are consistent with utility maximisation.

title: Slutsky Equation for Demand
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: The change in Marshallian demand caused by a price change decomposes into a substitution effect and an income effect.
latex: \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_j}-\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}x_j
short: Price changes shift both relative attractiveness and purchasing power.
detail: The substitution effect is negative semidefinite for the Hicksian demand.
proof: Differentiate the identity h(p,u(p,m)) = x(p,m) with respect to p_j using the envelope theorem.
consequence: It explains Giffen goods and the shape of demand curves.

title: Euler Equation of Optimal Consumption
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: In intertemporal consumption choice, the marginal utility of consuming today equals the discounted expected marginal utility of consuming tomorrow times the gross return on savings.
short: Consumers equalise the marginal value of saving and spending.
detail: Log utility with beta times the return less than one implies declining consumption when the return is high.
proof: Set up the Lagrangian for the two-period budget and differentiate with respect to current consumption.
consequence: It is the workhorse condition of growth and asset-pricing models.

title: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans Growth Model
subject: Mathematical Economics
statement: In the neoclassical growth model with optimising households, the economy converges to a steady-state capital stock where the modified golden-rule condition holds.
latex: \dot k=f(k)-c-(n+\delta)k,\qquad f'(k^*)=\rho+n+\delta\ \text{at the modified golden rule}
short: Saving, depreciation, and population growth balance in the long run.
detail: The discount rate makes steady-state capital lower than the golden-rule level when rho is positive.
proof: Solve the Hamiltonian system in (k,c), linearise around the steady state, and apply the transversality condition.
consequence: It explains long-run growth and capital accumulation without exogenous saving behaviour.

title: Black–Scholes Option Pricing Formula
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Under constant volatility and risk-free rate with no dividends, the price of a European call is given by a closed formula involving the standard normal distribution function.
short: Dynamic hedging removes risk and fixes the option price.
detail: The formula assumes frictionless markets and continuous trading.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to the option price and choose a delta-hedging portfolio whose drift equals the risk-free rate.
consequence: It founded modern derivatives pricing and risk management.

title: Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: A market has no arbitrage essentially if and only if there exists an equivalent martingale measure under which discounted asset prices are martingales.
latex: \text{no arbitrage}\iff \exists\ \mathbb Q\sim\mathbb P:\ e^{-rt}S_t\ \text{is a }\mathbb Q\text{-martingale}
short: Arbitrage-free prices are expectations under a risk-neutral measure.
detail: In incomplete markets the equivalent martingale measure need not be unique.
proof: Use the Hahn–Banach or separating hyperplane theorem to construct the pricing functional and show it defines a positive measure.
consequence: It links derivative pricing to martingale theory and completeness.

title: Put–Call Parity
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity and no dividends, the call price minus the put price equals the spot price minus the discounted strike.
short: A long call and short put replicate the underlying financed by borrowing.
detail: Dividends or foreign-currency carry modify the right-hand side by the present value of the dividend stream.
proof: At maturity both portfolios pay max(S_T-K,0)-max(K-S_T,0)=S_T-K; no-arbitrage then forces equality of initial values.
consequence: It detects arbitrage violations and links call and put markets.

title: Kalman Controllability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A finite-dimensional linear system is controllable exactly when the matrix formed from B, AB, ..., A^(n-1)B has full row rank.
short: Inputs must reach every mode of the system.
detail: The condition is equivalent to the observability of the transposed dual system.
proof: If the rank is deficient, an eigenvector of A^T orthogonal to the reachable subspace cannot be influenced; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the reachable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It decides whether pole placement and feedback design are possible.

title: Kalman Observability Rank Condition
subject: Control Theory
statement: A linear system is observable exactly when the stack of C, CA, ..., CA^(n-1) has full column rank.
short: Outputs must reveal every internal mode.
detail: Unobservable modes cannot be reconstructed from output histories but may still be stable.
proof: If O loses rank, there is a nonzero initial state producing zero output for all time; conversely the Cayley–Hamilton theorem shows the unobservable subspace is A-invariant.
consequence: It is the dual of controllability and governs state-estimator design.

title: Separation Principle for LQG Control
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with Gaussian noise and quadratic cost, an optimal output-feedback controller can be built by combining the optimal state-feedback law with an optimal state estimator, and the two designs can be carried out independently.
latex: u=-K\hat x,\qquad \hat x\ \text{from Kalman filter},\qquad J=J_{\text{LQR}}+J_{\text{est}}
short: Estimate first, then control as if the estimate were exact.
detail: The separation property relies on linearity, Gaussianity, and the quadratic cost.
proof: Use dynamic programming and the orthogonality of estimation error to the control history to factor the cost.
consequence: It makes stochastic optimal control computationally tractable.

title: Linear Quadratic Regulator and the Riccati Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear system with quadratic cost, the optimal feedback is u = -Kx where K comes from the stabilizing solution of the algebraic Riccati equation.
short: A matrix quadratic equation encodes the value function.
detail: Stabilizability and detectability guarantee existence of a unique stabilizing positive semidefinite solution.
proof: Substitute a quadratic value function V=x^TPx into the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and minimise over u.
consequence: It is the most widely used optimal control design method.

title: Kalman Filter as Optimal Linear Estimator
subject: Control Theory
statement: For a linear Gaussian state-space model, the Kalman filter recursively computes the conditional mean and covariance of the state given past observations, minimising mean-square error among all estimators.
short: Predict, compare with measurement, and blend by uncertainty.
detail: The gain can be interpreted as a least-squares weight between prediction and observation.
proof: Update the Gaussian conditional distribution using Bayes' rule and propagate its covariance through the linear dynamics.
consequence: It is the standard estimator in navigation, tracking, and time-series analysis.

title: Small-Gain Theorem for Feedback Stability
subject: Control Theory
statement: A feedback interconnection of two stable systems is stable if the product of their induced norms is strictly less than one.
short: The loop must not amplify signals around the cycle.
detail: General versions use gains in different induced norms or nonlinear gain functions.
proof: Write the closed-loop equations, take norms, and apply the contraction mapping principle when the loop gain is below one.
consequence: It is a central robust-stability tool for uncertain systems.

title: Lyapunov Equation for Linear Systems
subject: Control Theory
statement: A Hurwitz matrix A admits, for every positive definite Q, a unique positive definite solution P of the Lyapunov equation, and P certifies stability through the quadratic Lyapunov function x^T P x.
short: Solve a linear matrix equation to get a stability certificate.
detail: The continuous-time and discrete-time versions use different equations.
proof: Take P as an integral of exp(A^T t) Q exp(A t) over positive time and verify the equation by differentiation.
consequence: It provides computationally tractable stability tests and performance bounds.

title: BIBO Stability and Transfer Function Poles
subject: Control Theory
statement: A rational linear time-invariant system is bounded-input bounded-output stable exactly when all poles of its transfer function lie in the open left half-plane.
short: Stable poles mean bounded responses to bounded inputs.
detail: Unstable pole-zero cancellations can hide internal instability in the transfer function.
proof: The impulse response is a sum of decaying exponentials when poles are stable, so convolution with a bounded input stays bounded.
consequence: It connects time-domain stability with frequency-domain design.

title: Routh–Hurwitz Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: A real polynomial has all roots in the open left half-plane exactly when its Hurwitz determinants are all positive, equivalently when the Routh array has no sign changes in its first column.
short: Coefficients alone decide stability.
detail: Necessary conditions include all coefficients having the same sign.
proof: Construct the Hurwitz matrix from the coefficients and use the Cauchy index argument relating root locations to the signs of the determinants.
consequence: It tests stability without computing polynomial roots.

title: Nyquist Stability Criterion
subject: Control Theory
statement: The number of unstable poles of a closed-loop system is determined by the winding number of the open-loop frequency response around the point minus one.
short: Count encirclements to count unstable roots.
detail: The argument principle links the contour integral of the logarithm to zeros and poles.
proof: Apply the argument principle to 1+G(s) along a contour enclosing the right half-plane.
consequence: It provides gain and phase margin information for robust feedback design.

title: Pontryagin Maximum Principle
subject: Control Theory
statement: For an optimal control problem with state and control constraints, an optimal trajectory admits a costate satisfying adjoint equations and a maximisation condition on the Hamiltonian.
short: Optimality is a two-point boundary problem in state and costate.
detail: For normal problems the costate multiplier on the running cost is negative, and the Hamiltonian is constant when the dynamics are time-invariant.
proof: Apply a variational argument with needle perturbations of the control and use separation of the resulting cones.
consequence: It is the foundational necessary condition for optimal control.

title: Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equation
subject: Control Theory
statement: The value function of a continuous-time optimal control problem satisfies a nonlinear first-order PDE obtained by balancing immediate cost against the change in future value.
short: Dynamic programming becomes a partial differential equation.
detail: In deterministic quadratic problems it reduces to the Riccati equation; in stochastic settings a second-order term appears.
proof: Apply the dynamic programming principle over a vanishing time step and expand the value function to first order.
consequence: It connects optimal control, viscosity solutions, and reinforcement learning.

title: Complex Exponentials as LTI Eigenfunctions
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Every complex exponential is an eigenfunction of a linear time-invariant system, with eigenvalue given by the system's frequency response.
latex: x(t)=e^{i\omega t}\ \Rightarrow\ y(t)=H(i\omega)e^{i\omega t},\quad H(i\omega)=\int h(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}d\tau
short: Sinusoids pass through LTI systems unchanged except in amplitude and phase.
detail: The frequency response is the Fourier transform of the impulse response when it exists.
proof: Convolve the exponential with the impulse response and use translation to factor out e^{iomega t}.
consequence: Fourier analysis diagonalises LTI filtering and simplifies system design.

title: Butterworth Filter Magnitude Response
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A Butterworth filter has a magnitude response that is maximally flat in the passband and decreases monotonically to zero in the stopband.
short: No ripple in the passband, at the cost of a gentle roll-off.
detail: The order n sets the steepness; the cutoff omega_c is the half-power point.
proof: Choose a rational response whose first 2n-1 derivatives vanish at zero, giving a polynomial in omega^2 with a triple structure at the origin.
consequence: It is a standard baseline analog filter prototype.

title: Window Functions and Spectral Leakage
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Truncating a signal to a finite record convolves its spectrum with the Fourier transform of the window, spreading energy into neighbouring frequencies.
short: Finite observation smears sharp spectral lines.
detail: Rectangular windows have high sidelobes; Hann and Hamming windows trade resolution for sidelobe suppression.
proof: Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency by the convolution theorem.
consequence: Window choice controls bias and variance in spectral estimation.

title: Wiener Filter and Mean-Square Optimality
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For stationary signal and noise with known spectra, the linear filter minimising mean-square estimation error has a transfer function given by the signal spectrum divided by the total observed spectrum.
short: Pass frequencies where signal dominates noise.
detail: The causal version requires spectral factorisation of the observation spectrum.
proof: Write the mean-square error as an integral, complete the square pointwise in frequency, and choose H accordingly.
consequence: It is the classical optimum benchmark for denoising and equalisation.

title: Least Mean Squares Adaptive Filter
subject: Signal Processing
statement: The LMS algorithm updates filter coefficients by a small multiple of the instantaneous error times the input vector, approximating stochastic gradient descent on mean-square error.
short: Move the weights slightly against the observed error gradient.
detail: Convergence and misadjustment depend on the step size and input eigenvalue spread.
proof: The instantaneous gradient of the squared error is -2 e_n x_n; taking a single sample gives an unbiased stochastic gradient step.
consequence: It is simple and widely used in echo cancellation and adaptive equalisation.

title: Matched Filter and Signal-to-Noise Ratio
subject: Signal Processing
statement: For detecting a known waveform in additive white noise, the linear filter maximising output signal-to-noise ratio is matched to a time-reversed copy of the signal.
short: Correlate with the signal you expect.
detail: The maximum depends on signal energy but not on its detailed shape.
proof: Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the ratio of the filter output at the sampling time to the noise power.
consequence: It is the optimal receiver for known pulses in radar and communications.

title: Multiresolution Analysis and Wavelet Bases
subject: Signal Processing
statement: A multiresolution analysis is a nested sequence of approximation spaces whose differences yield wavelet subspaces, giving orthonormal bases localised in both scale and position.
latex: V_j\subset V_{j+1},\quad V_{j+1}=V_j\oplus W_j,\quad L^2=\bigoplus_j W_j
short: Approximations at one scale plus details at that scale build the next.
detail: Scaling functions generate V_j and wavelets generate W_j through dilation and translation.
proof: Construct the scaling filter satisfying quadrature-mirror conditions and verify orthonormality of the resulting dilates and translates.
consequence: It gives fast wavelet transforms and sparse representations of piecewise-smooth signals.

title: Total Variation Denoising
subject: Signal Processing
statement: Total variation denoising minimises a fidelity term plus a penalty on the total variation of the signal, suppressing noise while preserving sharp edges.
short: Penalise oscillation, not jumps.
detail: The solution has piecewise-smooth structure; in one dimension it can be computed exactly by the taut-string algorithm.
proof: Convexity gives a unique solution; optimality is expressed by the divergence of a dual field with modulus at most one.
consequence: It is a foundational method in image restoration and inverse problems.

title: Fisher Information Metric on Statistical Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Fisher information matrix defines a Riemannian metric on a parametric family of probability distributions, measuring distinguishability of nearby distributions.
short: Statistical distinguishability is a geometric distance.
detail: It equals the Hessian of the Kullback–Leibler divergence at coinciding parameters.
proof: Expand the KL divergence to second order in the parameter difference and identify the quadratic form.
consequence: It unifies statistics, information theory, and differential geometry.

title: Amari α-Connections and Dually Flat Manifolds
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A statistical manifold carries a one-parameter family of affine connections; the Levi-Civita connection corresponds to alpha zero, while alpha plus or minus one connections make exponential families dually flat.
short: Different connections capture different statistical structures.
detail: Dual flatness yields generalised Pythagorean theorems for divergences.
proof: Verify that the alpha connections are mutually dual with respect to the Fisher metric and that exponential families have vanishing alpha-one curvature.
consequence: It provides the language of information geometry for inference and optimisation.

title: Natural Gradient Descent
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Preconditioning a gradient by the inverse Fisher information makes optimisation steps invariant to reparametrisation of the statistical model.
short: Move a fixed distance in distribution space, not parameter space.
detail: It approximates steepest descent with respect to the Fisher–Rao metric.
proof: The Fisher metric transforms covariantly under reparametrisation, so the inverse-metric gradient transforms as a tangent vector.
consequence: It improves conditioning in probabilistic models and reinforcement learning.

title: Information Projection and Pythagorean Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In a dually flat statistical manifold, the KL divergence from an external point to its information projection onto a submanifold decomposes additively, giving a generalised Pythagorean theorem.
short: Projection onto a model splits divergence into two orthogonal parts.
detail: The cross term vanishes because the e-geodesic and m-geodesic meet orthogonally.
proof: Write the KL divergence in exponential-family coordinates and use the orthogonality of the dual geodesics.
consequence: It explains maximum likelihood as information projection and underlies EM geometry.

title: Itô's Lemma for Stochastic Differentials
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: For a smooth function of an Itô diffusion, the differential includes a second-order correction coming from quadratic variation.
short: Stochastic chains get an extra curvature term.
detail: The extra term vanishes for Stratonovich integrals but would make naive chain rule incorrect for Itô integrals.
proof: Taylor expand f, keep terms of order dt from the quadratic variation of Brownian motion, and pass to the limit in probability.
consequence: It is the master formula of stochastic calculus and option pricing.

title: Quadratic Variation of Brownian Motion
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Along a refining partition the sum of squared increments of Brownian motion converges in probability to the length of the time interval.
short: Brownian paths have infinite variation but finite quadratic variation.
detail: The convergence fails almost surely for arbitrary partitions but holds along refining deterministic partitions.
proof: Compute expectation and variance of the sum using independence of increments and the Gaussian second and fourth moments.
consequence: It creates the second-order term in Itô's formula and underlies realised volatility.

title: Itô Isometry
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The mean square of an Itô integral equals the expectation of the integral of the squared integrand.
short: Itô integrals preserve a scaled L^2 norm.
detail: The identity extends the definition of the integral from simple processes by completion.
proof: Verify it for simple adapted processes using independence of increments, then pass to limits by density.
consequence: It makes stochastic integration well defined on square-integrable adapted processes.

title: Stratonovich Integral and Chain Rule
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The Stratonovich stochastic integral obeys the ordinary chain rule and arises as the limit of integrals with midpoint evaluation.
short: Midpoint rules preserve the classical calculus identities.
detail: Conversion to Itô form introduces a correction term equal to half the derivative of the diffusion coefficient times its square.
proof: Compare left-endpoint and midpoint Riemann sums; the difference converges to half the quadratic covariation.
consequence: It is preferred in physical models where standard calculus rules should survive.

title: Girsanov Theorem and Measure Change
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: Under suitable integrability, shifting a Brownian motion by a drift can be absorbed by changing to an equivalent probability measure.
short: Drift is a matter of measure.
detail: Novikov's condition gives a simple sufficient condition for the density to be a true martingale.
proof: Use the stochastic exponential to define the density and verify the martingale property, then check the shifted process has Brownian quadratic variation and independent Gaussian increments.
consequence: It underlies risk-neutral pricing and importance sampling for diffusions.

title: Feynman–Kac Formula
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The solution of a parabolic PDE with a potential term can be represented as the expectation of a functional of a diffusion process.
short: Linear PDEs are averages over random paths.
detail: The generator of the diffusion supplies the second-order spatial operator.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to the product of the PDE solution and the exponential weight, then take expectations and use the martingale property.
consequence: It links PDE theory, stochastic processes, and Monte Carlo computation.

title: Fokker–Planck Equation
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The probability density of a diffusion solves a linear parabolic PDE whose adjoint is the backward Kolmogorov equation.
short: Probability mass flows by drift and diffuses by covariance.
detail: The stationary density solves the zero-flux equation when detailed balance holds.
proof: Apply Itô's lemma to a test function, take expectations, and integrate by parts to move derivatives onto the density.
consequence: It describes ensemble behaviour in statistical physics, biology, and finance.

title: Tanaka's Formula and Brownian Local Time
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The absolute value of Brownian motion minus its local time at zero is a martingale, generalising Itô's formula to a nonsmooth function.
short: Local time supplies the missing term at a kink.
detail: Local time measures the accumulated time the process spends near a given level, normalised by occupation density.
proof: Approximate the absolute value by smooth functions and use the occupation time formula to identify the limit of the second-derivative term.
consequence: It introduces local time and underpins the theory of reflected diffusions.

title: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Process and Stationary Distribution
subject: Stochastic Calculus
statement: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process is a mean-reverting diffusion with a Gaussian stationary distribution whose variance balances noise against restoring strength.
short: Noise and mean reversion reach a statistical equilibrium.
detail: Its correlation function decays exponentially with rate theta.
proof: Solve the linear SDE explicitly, compute mean and variance, and let time tend to infinity.
consequence: It models thermal fluctuations, interest rates, and velocity in Langevin dynamics.

title: Crystallographic Restriction Theorem
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A rotational symmetry compatible with a two- or three-dimensional periodic lattice can only have order 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6.
short: Lattices forbid fivefold and most other rotations.
detail: Quasicrystals evade the restriction by giving up periodicity.
proof: Take a shortest lattice vector and its rotation; their difference is a lattice vector whose length must be at least the minimum, forcing 2 cos theta to be an integer.
consequence: It classifies allowed crystal symmetries and motivated the discovery of quasicrystals.

title: The Seventeen Wallpaper Groups
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: There are exactly seventeen distinct plane crystallographic groups, classified by their translations, rotations, reflections, and glide reflections.
latex: p1,\ p2,\ pm,\ pg,\ cm,\ pmm,\ pmg,\ pgg,\ cmm,\ p4,\ p4m,\ p4g,\ p3,\ p3m1,\ p31m,\ p6,\ p6m
short: Repeating plane patterns fall into seventeen symmetry types.
detail: The classification combines the crystallographic restriction with the possible point groups and lattice shapes.
proof: Bound rotation orders by the crystallographic restriction and enumerate extensions of the translation lattice by the allowed point groups.
consequence: It classifies ornamental patterns and underlies computer vision models of texture.

title: The 230 Three-Dimensional Space Groups
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: There are 230 crystallographic space groups in three dimensions, obtained by combining the 32 point groups with 14 Bravais lattices and nonsymmorphic operations.
short: Three-dimensional crystal symmetry has a finite complete list.
detail: Eleven enantiomorphic pairs among them account for chiral crystal structures.
proof: Classify extensions of the translation group by point groups satisfying compatibility with the lattices, including screw axes and glide planes.
consequence: The list is the language of crystallographic databases and diffraction analysis.

title: Crystal Structure Factor and Electron Density
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The structure factor is the Fourier coefficient of the electron density, so diffraction intensities give its modulus while the phase must be recovered separately.
latex: F(\mathbf k)=\int \rho(\mathbf r)e^{2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}d\mathbf r,\qquad \rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_\mathbf k F(\mathbf k)e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}
short: Diffraction measures Fourier magnitudes of the crystal.
detail: The phase problem is the central obstacle in X-ray crystallography.
proof: Expand the periodic electron density in a Fourier series over the reciprocal lattice and identify coefficients with the scattered amplitudes.
consequence: Fourier inversion reconstructs molecular structures from diffraction data.

title: Bragg's Law of Diffraction
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Constructive reflection from crystal planes occurs when the path difference between waves reflected from successive planes equals an integer number of wavelengths.
short: Planes reflect strongly at angles matching their spacing.
detail: It is equivalent to the Laue condition that the scattering vector belongs to the reciprocal lattice.
proof: The extra path travelled by a ray reflecting from the next plane is 2d sin theta; require it to be an integer multiple of the wavelength.
consequence: It is the basic relation for measuring lattice spacings from diffraction angles.

title: Reciprocal Lattice and the Diffraction Pattern
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The reciprocal lattice consists of wave vectors giving plane waves periodic on the direct lattice, and diffraction peaks occur at those wave vectors.
latex: \mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij},\qquad \mathbf G=h\mathbf b_1+k\mathbf b_2+l\mathbf b_3
short: The diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the lattice.
detail: The spacing of reciprocal lattice points is inversely proportional to real-space spacing.
proof: A plane wave is periodic under all lattice translations exactly when its wave vector dotted with each lattice vector is a multiple of 2 pi.
consequence: It underlies indexing of diffraction peaks and electronic band structure.

title: Bloch's Theorem for Periodic Potentials
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Eigenfunctions of a Schrödinger operator with a periodic potential are plane waves modulated by a function with the periodicity of the lattice.
latex: \psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}u_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r),\qquad u(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=u(\mathbf r)
short: Periodic media have quasi-periodic eigenmodes.
detail: The crystal momentum k is defined modulo reciprocal lattice vectors.
proof: The translation operators commute with the Hamiltonian, so simultaneous eigenfunctions exist and their translation eigenvalues have modulus one.
consequence: It reduces band-structure calculations to a single unit cell.

title: Brillouin Zones and Band Gaps
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The first Brillouin zone is the Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice; energy bands of a periodic Schrödinger operator can have gaps at its boundaries.
latex: BZ=\{\mathbf k:|\mathbf k|\le|\mathbf k-\mathbf G|\ \forall \mathbf G\ne0\}
short: Bragg reflection at zone boundaries opens spectral gaps.
detail: Degenerate plane waves coupled by a reciprocal lattice vector split in energy.
proof: Restrict the eigenproblem to a two-wave approximation at a zone boundary and diagonalise the resulting two-by-two matrix.
consequence: It explains conductors, semiconductors, and insulators in terms of band structure.

title: Penrose Tilings and Quasicrystalline Order
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Penrose tilings are nonperiodic but ordered planar tilings with sharp diffraction peaks and fivefold symmetry, serving as models for quasicrystals.
short: Order need not imply periodicity.
detail: Their Fourier spectra contain Bragg peaks at a dense set of wave vectors.
proof: Use the substitution rule based on the golden ratio to build arbitrarily large patches and analyse their Fourier–Bohr spectrum.
consequence: They overturned the assumption that crystals must be periodic.

title: Hückel Molecular Orbital Method
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In the Hückel approximation, pi-electron molecular orbitals are eigenvectors of a weighted adjacency matrix of the carbon skeleton, with eigenvalues giving orbital energies.
short: Spectral graph theory predicts conjugated-molecule orbitals.
detail: Only nearest-neighbour carbon interactions are retained, and overlap integrals are neglected.
proof: Write the linear combination of atomic orbitals equations, set Coulomb integrals to alpha and neighbour resonance integrals to beta, and diagonalise.
consequence: It connects graph spectra to aromatic stability and electron transitions.

title: Pólya Enumeration of Chemical Isomers
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Burnside's lemma and cycle-index generating functions count distinct molecular structures up to the symmetry group of the molecular graph.
short: Average fixed colourings to count unlabelled structures.
detail: Pólya's theorem refines the count by tracking the numbers of each substituent.
proof: Count colourings fixed by each group element and average over the group using Burnside's lemma.
consequence: It automates isomer enumeration in computational chemistry.

title: Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness (Open)
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with smooth initial data, global existence of smooth solutions is not known; weak solutions exist but their uniqueness and regularity remain open.
short: The fundamental regularity question for 3D fluid flow is unresolved.
detail: Existence of finite-energy weak solutions was proved by Leray; the missing step is ruling out finite-time singularities.
proof: Open. Leray constructed global weak solutions via Galerkin approximations and energy estimates; whether they remain smooth is unknown, and the problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.
consequence: Resolution would transform the mathematical foundations of fluid mechanics.

title: Euler Equations of Inviscid Fluid Flow
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Euler equations express conservation of mass, momentum, and energy for a nonviscous compressible fluid as a system of hyperbolic conservation laws.
short: Newton's laws written for a continuous inviscid medium.
detail: An equation of state closes the system by relating pressure, density, and energy.
proof: Apply integral conservation laws to an arbitrary material volume and use the divergence theorem.
consequence: It is the starting point for compressible aerodynamics and shock-wave theory.

title: Kelvin Circulation Theorem
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: In an inviscid barotropic flow with conservative body forces, the circulation around a material loop is conserved as the loop moves with the fluid.
short: Vortex lines are frozen into an ideal fluid.
detail: Viscosity, non-barotropic thermodynamics, or nonconservative forces break the conservation.
proof: Differentiate the line integral along the material loop, use the Euler equations, and convert the integrand to a perfect differential.
consequence: It underlies vortex dynamics and the persistence of lift in ideal flow.

title: Bernoulli's Theorem for Steady Inviscid Flow
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Along a streamline of a steady inviscid incompressible flow in a conservative force field, the sum of pressure head, kinetic head, and potential head is constant.
short: Pressure drops where speed rises.
detail: For irrotational flow the constant is the same on all streamlines.
proof: Project the steady Euler equations along the velocity direction and integrate along the streamline.
consequence: It explains lift, venturi meters, and the pressure distribution around airfoils.

title: Reynolds Number and Dynamic Similarity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The dimensionless Reynolds number comparing inertial to viscous forces determines whether geometrically similar flows behave alike.
short: Same Reynolds number means dynamically similar flow.
detail: Low Reynolds number flows are laminar and viscosity-dominated; high Reynolds number flows develop turbulence and thin boundary layers.
proof: Nondimensionalise the Navier–Stokes equations using a length U and velocity scale U, leaving the coefficient 1/Re on the viscous term.
consequence: It justifies wind-tunnel scaling and organises empirical flow regimes.

title: Shallow Water Equations
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The shallow water equations model a thin layer of fluid under gravity by coupling depth-averaged momentum to mass conservation, forming a hyperbolic system with wave speed sqrt(gh).
short: Long gravity waves travel at speed sqrt(g times depth).
detail: They admit shocks interpreted as hydraulic jumps and bore waves.
proof: Integrate the incompressible Euler equations over the thin layer and assume hydrostatic pressure and small vertical acceleration.
consequence: They model tides, tsunamis, and river flooding.

title: Korteweg–de Vries Soliton
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Korteweg–de Vries equation admits solitary travelling waves whose speed is proportional to their amplitude and which survive collisions almost unchanged.
short: Dispersion balances nonlinearity to create a stable pulse.
detail: The equation is integrable and possesses an infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities.
proof: Insert the travelling-wave ansatz, integrate twice using decay at infinity, and verify the sech-squared profile.
consequence: It founded soliton theory with applications to water waves and fibre optics.

title: Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation and Bright Solitons
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation supports bright solitons whose dispersion is exactly balanced by self-focusing nonlinearity.
short: Self-focusing traps the wave against spreading.
detail: The defocusing sign instead supports dark solitons on a nonzero background.
proof: Insert the ansatz into the equation and match real and imaginary parts, using the sech differential equation.
consequence: It models optical fibres, Bose–Einstein condensates, and deep-water envelopes.

title: Burgers' Equation and Shock Formation
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The viscous Burgers equation combines nonlinear steepening with diffusion; in the inviscid limit it develops shock waves selected by the entropy condition.
short: Nonlinearity sharpens waves while viscosity smooths them.
detail: The Cole–Hopf transform linearises the viscous equation to the heat equation.
proof: Set u = -2 nu (phi_x/phi) to reduce Burgers to the heat equation for phi, then study the zero-viscosity limit.
consequence: It is the simplest model for shock formation and turbulence analogies.

title: Rankine–Hugoniot Conditions
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Across a shock discontinuity, conservation laws require the jump in flux to equal the shock speed times the jump in the conserved quantity.
short: Conservation dictates how fast a discontinuity can move.
detail: An additional entropy condition selects the admissible branch of solutions.
proof: Integrate the conservation law over a shrinking space-time pillbox around the shock and let its width tend to zero.
consequence: It determines shock speeds in gas dynamics and traffic flow.

title: Helmholtz Equation and the Sommerfeld Radiation Condition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Time-harmonic wave scattering is governed by the Helmholtz equation, and outgoing solutions are selected by requiring decay of the radial derivative in the far field.
short: The radiation condition forbids waves arriving from infinity.
detail: It ensures uniqueness for exterior boundary value problems at real wave numbers.
proof: Expand the solution in outgoing Hankel functions and show the condition excludes the incoming branch.
consequence: It is essential for well-posed acoustic and electromagnetic scattering problems.
